title: Who you are
sub: Je suis, tu es, vous êtes
can: Greet people, say who you are and where you are from, and choose between tu and vous.
doneText: You can now greet someone, introduce yourself, say where you are from and pick tu or vous.

discover.intro: All of these sentences ask a question. Spot why some use tu and others use vous. The English tells you who is being asked.

groups.label: Blue
lines: Are you a student? (asking a classmate)
Where are you from? (asking a child)

groups.label: Orange
lines: Are you a teacher? (asking an adult you have just met)
Where are you from? (asking a friend's parents)

discover.question: Why tu in blue and vous in orange?
options: Tu is for people you know well and children. Vous is for strangers and anyone you want to be polite to.
Tu is for men and vous is for women.
Tu is for questions and vous is for statements.
discover.nudge: Not quite. Read who is being asked in the English, in each colour.
discover.reveal: Tu is for friends, family, children and people your age in a relaxed setting. Vous is for strangers, shop staff, older people and anyone you want to be polite to. Vous is also what you say to more than one person. The verb changes with them too. Here is être, to be:

learn.title: Être and polite words
learn.sub: Tap any form to hear it

blocks.text: On is the everyday word for we: on est à Paris means we are in Paris. It uses the same verb form as il and elle.
When a short word meets a vowel, it drops its last letter and takes an apostrophe: je m'appelle, d'où, c'est. Say it as one flowing word.

blocks.title: Tu or vous
a: Are you a student? (to a friend)
b: Are you a student? (to a stranger, or to several people)
blocks.note: If you are not sure, use vous. When it is fine to use tu, people will say on peut se tutoyer, we can use tu. Young people often use tu straight away.

blocks.text: After je suis, a job has no a or an: je suis professeur, not je suis un professeur. Nationalities have a small letter: elle est anglaise. For a woman, many words add an e: étudiant, étudiante.

In France, say bonjour when you walk into a shop, café or lift, and au revoir when you leave. Walking in without a greeting is rude. Friends greet with la bise, a kiss on each cheek, and how many varies by region. With new people, shake hands.

phrases.en: How are you? How's it going?

exercises.prompt: You ask an older woman you have just met if she is French. Which is right?
exercises.why: A stranger or an older person gets vous: vous êtes française ?
Il, elle and on all go with est.
Bonsoir means good evening. Bonjour is for the day.

items.why: On takes the same form as il: est.

exercises.prompt: Tap the word that is wrong.
exercises.why: Tu goes with es. Êtes goes with vous.

exercises.prompt: Tap the word that is wrong.

exercises.why: Je suis français for a man, je suis française for a woman.

exercises.q: To a stranger: are you English?
exercises.why: A stranger gets vous: vous êtes anglais, or anglaise for a woman.

exercises.q: To a friend: where are you from?
exercises.why: Tu es d'où ? is the everyday way to ask.

exercises.prompt: Nice to meet you, I'm British.
exercises.why: Greet first, then je suis plus the nationality, with no a or an.

exercises.prompt: You walk into a small bakery in France. What do you do first?
exercises.why: Say bonjour first. Skipping it is rude in France.
Where you are from uses de: je suis de Londres. Before a vowel it becomes d': je suis d'Écosse.
Je m'appelle means my name is. Literally, I call myself.
Au revoir, literally until we see again.

write.title: Say it in your own words
write.task: Introduce yourself to someone new in France: say your name, that you are British, and ask where they are from.
write.starter: Bonjour, je m'appelle…  Je suis…  Vous êtes d'où ?
write.model: Bonjour, je m'appelle {name}. Je suis britannique. Et vous, vous êtes d'où ?
checklist: Je suis plus your nationality, with no a or an
Vous for a stranger, tu for a friend

boss.title: Meeting Madame Roux in Lyon
boss.persona: You are Madame Roux, a friendly landlady in Lyon. The learner has just arrived as your new tenant. Greet them, ask their name, where they are from and whether they are a student. Address the learner as vous. Keep every message to one short sentence.

choices: Salut is for friends. With a landlady you have just met, say bonjour and madame.
Oui, bonjour. Tu es madame Roux ?
Use vous with someone you do not know: vous êtes madame Roux ?
Je goes with suis: je suis britannique.
No a or an before a nationality: je suis britannique.

turns.en: Very good. Are you a student?
choices: No a or an after je suis with a job: je suis professeur.
Tu es means you are. For I am, say je suis.

turns.npc: Parfait. Voici la clé, {name}. À demain.
turns.en: Perfect. Here is the key, {name}. See you tomorrow.
choices: Bonjour is for hello. When you leave, say au revoir or à demain.
Salut is for friends. Say au revoir or à demain to a landlady.
